The contribution to the grand potential from the pseudo-fermionic charge sector is found as

ΩH​F​C,c,f(2)=−2​zH​F​C,c,f​z¯​ε0.\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,c,f}=-2z_{HFC,c,f}\overline{z}\varepsilon_{0}. (99)

In total, the HFC to the grand potential may be summed up to give

ΩH​F​C(2)=−U/2+3(β0−α)+ΩH​F​C,3​s,f(2)+ΩH​F​C,c,f(2).\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC}=-U/2+3(\beta_{0}-\alpha)+\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,3s,f}+\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,c,f}. (100)

The correction turns out to be substantial, of the order of the mean field Ω(0)\Omega^{(0)}.

Appendix E Free bosons

In this section, we display the working of the evaluation of the functional integral representation of the partition function in terms of CT approach plus HFC in a most simple example, a free boson system. The Hamiltonian for free bosons in quantum states labeled by α\alpha is given by

H^=∑αϵα​bα†​bα.\hat{H}=\sum_{\alpha}\epsilon_{\alpha}\,b_{\alpha}^{\dagger}b_{\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}. (101)

In the following, we determine the grand potential of this system from its functional integral representation in three different ways and recover the same, well-known result. The first two approaches are textbook-knowledge, i.e., (i) the rigorous calculation in discrete imaginary time and (ii) complex integration in the CT limit with an adequate convergence parameter to cure the ill-defined limit to continuous time. Both methods are hard to generalize to the numerical evaluation of non-analytically solvable models. Lastly, we (iii) evaluate the grand potential in the CT limit without a convergence parameter and recover the correct result with the addition of high frequency contributions (HFC). This approach is in close analogy to our approach of calculating fluctuation corrections to the grand potential of the Hubbard model described in this paper.

E.1 Discrete imaginary time

Within the exact discrete imaginary-time path integral, the partition function is given by Eq. (21) with the action in Eq. (22). After integration of the fields, the partition function is found to be the inverse action determinant

Z=∏αlimM→∞(detS)α−1,Z=\prod_{\alpha}\lim_{M\rightarrow\infty}\left(\det S\right)_{\alpha}^{-1}, (102)

where the SS is represented by the M×MM\times M matrix

S\displaystyle S =(100⋯0−γ−γ1000−γ1⋱0−γ⋱0⋱00−γ1),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&\cdots&0&-\gamma\\ -\gamma&1&0&&&0\\ 0&-\gamma&1&\ddots&&\vdots\\ \vdots&0&-\gamma&\ddots&\\ &&0&\ddots&&0\\ 0&&&&-\gamma&1\\ \end{pmatrix}, (103a)
with
γ\displaystyle\gamma =1−βM​ϵα,\displaystyle=1-\frac{\beta}{M}\epsilon_{\alpha}, (103b)
and MM is the number of time slices. By Laplace expansion of the first row, the determinant is found to be
detS\displaystyle\det S =1+(−1)M−1​(−γ)M.\displaystyle=1+(-1)^{M-1}(-\gamma)^{M}. (103c)
Evaluating the limit of infinite time slices, the partition function of free particles is found to be
Z\displaystyle Z =∏α(1−e−β​ϵα)−1,\displaystyle=\prod_{\alpha}\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\beta\epsilon_{\alpha}}\right)^{-1}, (103d)

yielding the well-known result

Ω=−T​ln⁡Z=T​∑αln⁡(1−e−β​ϵα).\Omega=-T\ln Z=T\sum_{\alpha}\ln\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\beta\epsilon_{\alpha}}\right). (104)

E.2 Continuous imaginary time with convergence factor

In the CT limit, the action is diagonalized by Fourier transformation to Matsubara space and given by

S=T​∑α∑i​ωnbn,α∗​(−i​ωn+ϵα)​bn,α.S=T\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\mathrm{i}\omega_{n}}b^{*}_{n,\alpha}(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{n}+\epsilon_{\alpha})b_{n,\alpha}. (105)

By integrating out the fields bn,αb_{n,\alpha}, we find the partition function

Z=∏α∏ωn1−i​ωn+ϵα,Z=\prod_{\alpha}\prod_{\omega_{n}}\frac{1}{-\mathrm{i}\omega_{n}+\epsilon_{\alpha}}, (106)

which is formally divergent due to the ill-defined continuum limit. The correct result for the grand potential can be recovered by mapping onto a complex contour integral and the addition of the convergence factor eωn​0+\mathrm{e}^{\omega_{n}0^{+}}:

Ω=T​∑α,nln⁡(−i​ωn+ϵα)​ei​ωn​0+=−∑α∮d​z2​π​inB(z)ln(ϵα−z)ez​0+=−∑α∫−∞∞d​ω2​π​inB(ω)[ln(ϵα−ω+i0+)−ln(ϵα−ω−i0+)]=−∑α∫−∞∞d​ω2​π​inB(ω)2πiΘ(ω−ϵα)=−∑α∫ϵα∞dωnB(ω)=T​∑αln⁡(1−e−β​ϵα).\displaystyle\begin{split}\Omega&=T\sum_{\alpha,n}\ln(-i\omega_{n}+\epsilon_{\alpha})\mathrm{e}^{i\omega_{n}0^{+}}\\ &=-\sum_{\alpha}\oint\frac{dz}{2\pi i}n_{B}(z)\ln\left(\epsilon_{\alpha}-z\right)\mathrm{e}^{z0^{+}}\\ &=-\sum_{\alpha}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}n_{B}(\omega)\left[\ln\left(\epsilon_{\alpha}-\omega+i0^{+}\right)-\ln\left(\epsilon_{\alpha}-\omega-i0^{+}\right)\right]\\ &=-\sum_{\alpha}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}n_{B}(\omega)2\pi\mathrm{i}\ \Theta\left(\omega-\epsilon_{\alpha}\right)=-\sum_{\alpha}\int_{\epsilon_{\alpha}}^{\infty}d\omega n_{B}(\omega)\\ &=T\sum_{\alpha}\ln\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\beta\epsilon_{\alpha}}\right).\end{split} (107)

E.3 Continuous imaginary time with high frequency contributions

In close analogy to the d1,d2d_{1},d_{2} fields in the SB formalism, we now decompose the bosonic operators for the free boson Hamiltonian into their real and imaginary part b=b1+i​b2b=b_{1}+\mathrm{i}b_{2}. This way, the action can be represented by a 2×22\times 2 matrix

𝒮=∑α∑i​ωn(b1∗b2∗)​(ϵαωn−ωnϵα)​(b1b2),\mathcal{S}=\sum_{\alpha}\sum_{\mathrm{i}\omega_{n}}\begin{pmatrix}b_{1}^{*}&b_{2}^{*}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\epsilon_{\alpha}&\omega_{n}\\ -\omega_{n}&\epsilon_{\alpha}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}b_{1}\\ b_{2}\end{pmatrix}, (108)

whose determinant

D⁡(ωn)=ϵα2+ωn2=(ϵα+i​ωn)​(ϵα−i​ωn)D(\omega_{n})=\epsilon_{\alpha}^{2}+\omega_{n}^{2}=(\epsilon_{\alpha}+\mathrm{i}\omega_{n})(\epsilon_{\alpha}-\mathrm{i}\omega_{n}) (109)

is an even function in ωn\omega_{n} like the fluctuation determinant detℳ\det\mathcal{M}. The partition function is given by

Z=∏α∏ωn1D⁡(ωn),Z=\prod_{\alpha}\prod_{\omega_{n}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{D(\omega_{n})}}, (110)

the square root is added because the determinant D⁡(ω)D(\omega) is already a product of positive and negative Matsubara frequencies such that there would be an over-counting otherwise in this basis. The grand potential is thus given by

ΩC​T=T​∑α12​∑i​ωnln⁡D⁡(ωn).\Omega_{CT}=T\sum_{\alpha}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\ln D(\omega_{n}). (111)

In full analogy to the procedure discussed in subsection IV.2, the Matsubara sum is mapped onto a complex contour integral. After integration by parts, one finds

Ω=12​∑α∫−∞∞d​ωπ​f​(ω)​S​(ω),\Omega=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{\pi}f(\omega)S(\omega), (112)

where

f⁡(ω)\displaystyle f(\omega) =ω2+Tln|1−e−ω/T|,\displaystyle=\frac{\omega}{2}+T\ln\Big|1-\mathrm{e}^{-\omega/T}\Big|, (113)
S⁡(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle S({\bm{q}},\omega) =−D′∂ωD′′+D′′∂ωD′|D|2,\displaystyle=\frac{-D^{\prime}\partial_{\omega}D^{\prime\prime}+D^{\prime\prime}\partial_{\omega}D^{\prime}}{|D|^{2}}, (114)

with D=D′+i​D′′D=D^{\prime}+iD^{\prime\prime} within the analytic continuation i​ωn→ω+i​η\mathrm{i}\omega_{n}\rightarrow\omega+i\eta and η→0+\eta\rightarrow 0^{+}. For the determinant of free bosons, the distribution of bosonic excitations is given by

S⁡(ω)\displaystyle S(\omega) =limη→0ηη2+(ωn−ϵα2)+ηη2+(ωn+ϵα2)\displaystyle=\lim_{\eta\rightarrow 0}\frac{\eta}{\eta^{2}+(\omega_{n}-\epsilon_{\alpha}^{2})}+\frac{\eta}{\eta^{2}+(\omega_{n}+\epsilon_{\alpha}^{2})} (115)
=π​δ​(ω−ϵα)+π​δ​(ω+ϵα).\displaystyle=\pi\delta(\omega-\epsilon_{\alpha})+\pi\delta(\omega+\epsilon_{\alpha}). (116)

Since the integrand is a symmetric function in ω\omega, we can rewrite the integral boundaries

ΩC​T=∑α∫0∞d​ωπ​f​(ω)​S​(ω)=∑αϵα2+T​∑αln⁡(1−e−β​ϵα).\Omega_{CT}=\sum_{\alpha}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{\pi}f(\omega)S(\omega)=\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\epsilon_{\alpha}}{2}+T\sum_{\alpha}\ln\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\beta\epsilon_{\alpha}}\right). (117)

Compared to the previous approaches, we have the additional zero-point energy ∑αϵα2\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\epsilon_{\alpha}}{2}, which is not present in the exact discrete-time result. This is due to the ill-defined continuum limit. The high frequency contributions (HFC) described in subsection IV.3 are given by the commutator

ΩH​F​C=12∑αϵα[b†,b]=−12∑αϵα.\Omega_{HFC}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}\epsilon_{\alpha}[b^{\dagger},b]=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}\epsilon_{\alpha}. (118)

Therefore, we recover the correct result

Ω=ΩC​T+ΩH​F​C=T​∑αln⁡(1−e−β​ϵα).\Omega=\Omega_{CT}+\Omega_{HFC}=T\sum_{\alpha}\ln\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\beta\epsilon_{\alpha}}\right). (119)

This demonstrates the effectiveness of the HFC by correctly complementing the CT result in an analytically controlled example.

Appendix F Non-interacting limit (U=0U=0)

Here, we show that the non-interacting limit (U=0)(U=0), where the analytic solution of the Hubbard model is available, is fully recovered within the presented KR slave-boson mean field and fluctuation formalism (SRIKR+). Specifically, in this limit, (i) the MF saddle point recovers the exact solution, (ii) the fluctuation corrections to the ground-state energy vanish, and (iii) the dynamic spin χs​(q)\chi_{s}(q) and charge susceptibility χc​(q)\chi_{c}(q) reduce to the bare susceptibility χ0​(q)\chi_{0}(q), which is the expected behavior.

For free electrons that obey the Pauli principle, the states |↑⟩\left|\uparrow\right\rangle, |↓⟩\left|\downarrow\right\rangle are occupied randomly with the same probability on each lattice site. For an average filling of nn per site, where 0≤n≤20\leq n\leq 2, the mean occupation of both states is given by n/2n/2, respectively. Consequently, the average number of doubly occupied states is given by d2=(n/2)2d^{2}=(n/2)^{2}. The mean value of the density of singly occupied sites yields p02=2​(n/2)​(1−n/2)p_{0}^{2}=2(n/2)(1-n/2) by accounting for the spin degeneracy. Finally, we find e2=1−d2−p02=(1−n/2)2e^{2}=1-d^{2}-p_{0}^{2}=(1-n/2)^{2}. The MF values derived from this simple argument are consistent with the analytic solution presented in Eq. (54). Moreover, the Lagrange multiplier β0\beta_{0} vanishes at U=0U=0, whereas α\alpha remains finite and is a positive definite quantity. In summary, the density-dependent MF solution in the non-interacting limit is given by

e=1−n2,p0=n⁡(1−n2),d=n2,𝒑=0,β0=0,𝜷=0,α=4n⁡(2−n)​ε0,\displaystyle\begin{split}e&=1-\frac{n}{2},\,p_{0}=\sqrt{n\left(1-\frac{n}{2}\right)},\,d=\frac{n}{2},\,{\bm{p}}=0,\\ \beta_{0}&=0,\,{\bm{\beta}}=0,\\ \alpha&=\frac{4}{n(2-n)}\varepsilon_{0},\end{split} (120)

where ε0\varepsilon_{0} has been defined in Eq. (36). Within the MF ansatz, the Kotliar-Ruckenstein renormalized hopping amplitude defined in Eq. (3) reduces to

z0=p0​(e+d)2​(1−d2−p02/2)​(1−e2−p02/2)=1|U=0z_{0}=\frac{p_{0}(e+d)}{\sqrt{2(1-d^{2}-p_{0}^{2}/2)(1-e^{2}-p_{0}^{2}/2)}}=1\Bigg|_{U=0} (121)

and is equal to unity employing the values for the boson amplitudes given in Eq. (120) (equivalent to the values cited above) for arbitrary filling nn. Thus, the non-interacting limit is exactly fulfilled on MF level. For fluctuations around PM saddle points, the spin and charge sectors are decoupled and independently satisfy the exact non-interacting limit, as we show in the following.

F.1 Spin sector

With Eq. (120), we can evaluate all zz-factor derivatives that appear in the fluctuation calculation such that the results depend solely on nn. We find z~+,p1​p1=z~−,p1=0\tilde{z}_{+,p_{1}p_{1}}=\tilde{z}_{-,p_{1}}=0 for arbitrary filling such that the spin fluctuation matrix given by Eq. (71) simplifies to

ℳs​(q)|U=0=(0−p¯0−p¯0−χ0(q)/2).\mathcal{M}_{s}(q)\Big|_{U=0}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\overline{p}_{0}\\ -\overline{p}_{0}&-\chi_{0}(q)/2\end{pmatrix}. (122)

Consequently, the spin susceptibility

χs​(q)=2​p¯02​ℳp1​p1−1=χ0​(q)|U=0,\chi_{s}(q)=2\overline{p}_{0}^{2}\mathcal{M}^{-1}_{p_{1}p_{1}}=\chi_{0}(q)\Big|_{U=0}, (123)

reduces to the bare susceptibility χ0​(q)\chi_{0}(q) as it is expected in the non-interacting limit.

F.1.1 Continuous time contribution

The spin determinant

detℳs|U=0=−p02\det\mathcal{M}_{s}\Big|_{U=0}=-p_{0}^{2} (124)

does not depend on ωn\omega_{n} such that the CT contribution to the grand potential given by Eq. (33) vanishes

ΩC​T,s(2)|U=0=0.\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,s}\Big|_{U=0}=0. (125)

Notice that the sign of the determinant depends on the integration path of the Lagrange multipliers. The results given here correspond to integration along the real axis, while the Lagrange multipliers β0\beta_{0} and 𝜷{\bm{\beta}} actually need to be integrated through the saddle point along the imaginary axis. This changes the fluctuation matrix according to ℳμ,βν→i​ℳμ,βν,ℳβ,μν→i​ℳβ,μν\mathcal{M}_{\mu,\beta_{\nu}}\rightarrow\mathrm{i}\mathcal{M}_{\mu,\beta_{\nu}},\mathcal{M}_{\beta,\mu_{\nu}}\rightarrow\mathrm{i}\mathcal{M}_{\beta,\mu_{\nu}} and ℳβν,βν→−ℳβν,βν\mathcal{M}_{\beta_{\nu},\beta_{\nu}}\rightarrow-\mathcal{M}_{\beta_{\nu},\beta_{\nu}}, where ν=0,1,2,3\nu=0,1,2,3. With that applied, the spin determinant changes its sign and is positive definite as expected for stable saddle points. Since the susceptibilities and fluctuation corrections are independent of this transformation, we kept the fluctuation matrix in the convention that was applied in previous works.

F.1.2 High frequency contribution

According to Eq. (35), the HFC contribution

ΩH​F​C,s(2)\displaystyle\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,s} =−32​(α−β0)−2​zH​F​C,3​s​z0​ε0\displaystyle=-\frac{3}{2}\left(\alpha-\beta_{0}\right)-2z_{HFC,3s}z_{0}\varepsilon_{0} (126)
=−32​α+6n⁡(2−n)​ε0|U=0=0\displaystyle=-\frac{3}{2}\alpha+\frac{6}{n(2-n)}\varepsilon_{0}\Big|_{U=0}=0 (127)

vanishes for any filling nn in the non-interacting limit, which can be verified by inserting Eq. (122) into the expression for zH​F​C,3​sz_{HFC,3s} given by Eq. (37). Thus, there are no spin fluctuation contributions at U=0U=0.

F.2 Charge sector

For the intricate charge fluctuation matrix derived in Appendix B, there are extensive simplifications at U=0U=0 because the first derivatives vanish z~d1=z~p0=0\tilde{z}_{d_{1}}=\tilde{z}_{p_{0}}=0. This can be directly inferred from the MF saddle point equations ∂Ω(0)/∂ψμ=0\partial\Omega^{(0)}/\partial\psi_{\mu}=0, where α\alpha does not enter because of the substitution of the ee-field and β0=0\beta_{0}=0 such that only the pseudofermionic part proportional to the derivative remains. Notice that zd1≠0z_{d_{1}}\neq 0, zp0≠0z_{p_{0}}\neq 0 because α\alpha enters the saddle point equations without the substitution of the ee-field (or any other field). The derivatives wrt. d2d_{2} do not vanish but are purely imaginary and yield z~d2=i\tilde{z}_{d_{2}}=i, z~d2∗=−i\tilde{z}^{*}_{d_{2}}=-i for any nn. The second derivatives are density dependent and can be evaluated with Eq. (120). Consequently, the charge fluctuation matrix given by Eq. (73) is simplified to

ℳc​(q)|U=0=(−ε0​z~d1​d1ωn−ε0​z~d1​p0−n−ωn−ε0​(1+z~d2​d2)+12​ωn2​χ0​(q)0−12​ωn​χ0​(q)−ε0​z~d1​d10−ε0​z~p0​p0−n⁡(1−n2)−n12​ωn​χ0−n⁡(1−n2)−12​χ0​(q)),\mathcal{M}_{c}(q)\Big|_{U=0}=\begin{pmatrix}-\varepsilon_{0}\tilde{z}_{d_{1}d_{1}}&\omega_{n}&-\varepsilon_{0}\tilde{z}_{d_{1}p_{0}}&-n\\ -\omega_{n}&-\varepsilon_{0}(1+\tilde{z}_{d_{2}d_{2}})+\frac{1}{2}\omega_{n}^{2}\,\chi_{0}(q)&0&-\frac{1}{2}\omega_{n}\,\chi_{0}(q)\\ -\varepsilon_{0}\tilde{z}_{d_{1}d_{1}}&0&-\varepsilon_{0}\tilde{z}_{p_{0}p_{0}}&-\sqrt{n(1-\frac{n}{2})}\\ -n&\frac{1}{2}\omega_{n}\,\chi_{0}&-\sqrt{n(1-\frac{n}{2})}&-\frac{1}{2}\chi_{0}(q)\end{pmatrix}, (128)

where

z~d1​d1\displaystyle\tilde{z}_{d_{1}d_{1}} =−16​(1−n)2(2−n)3​n,\displaystyle=-\frac{16(1-n)^{2}}{(2-n)^{3}n}, (129)
z~d1​p0\displaystyle\tilde{z}_{d_{1}p_{0}} =16​(1−n)(2−n)​(2−n)3​2​n,\displaystyle=\frac{16(1-n)}{(2-n)\sqrt{(2-n)^{3}2n}}, (130)
z~d2​d2\displaystyle\tilde{z}_{d_{2}d_{2}} =−2n,\displaystyle=-\frac{2}{n}, (131)
z~p0​d0\displaystyle\tilde{z}_{p_{0}d_{0}} =−8(2−n)2.\displaystyle=-\frac{8}{(2-n)^{2}}. (132)

The charge susceptibility is given by

χc​(q)\displaystyle\chi_{c}(q) =8​d¯2​ℳd1,d1−1​(q)+2​p¯02​ℳp0,p0−1​(q)+4​d¯​p¯0​ℳd1,p0−1​(q)\displaystyle=8\overline{d}^{2}\mathcal{M}_{d_{1},d_{1}}^{-1}(q)+2\overline{p}_{0}^{2}\mathcal{M}_{p_{0},p_{0}}^{-1}(q)+4\overline{d}_{\phantom{0}}\overline{p}_{0}\mathcal{M}_{d_{1},p_{0}}^{-1}(q)
=χ0​(q)|U=0,\displaystyle=\chi_{0}(q)\Big|_{U=0}, (133)

and thus reduces to the bare susceptibility in analogy to the spin sector. We confirmed that this result is basis-independent; it is also recovered within the basis of complex fields d∗,dd^{*},d rather than the decomposition in real and imaginary part d1,d2d_{1},d_{2} that we apply.

F.2.1 Continuous time contribution

The charge determinant inferred from Eq. (128)

detℳc​(ωn)|U=0=n⁡(n−2)2​[(4​ϵ0n⁡(n−2))2+ωn2]=−p02​(α2+ωn2)\displaystyle\begin{split}\det\mathcal{M}_{c}(\omega_{n})\Big|_{U=0}&=\frac{n(n-2)}{2}\left[\left(\frac{4\epsilon_{0}}{n(n-2)}\right)^{2}+\omega_{n}^{2}\right]\\ &=-p_{0}^{2}\left(\alpha^{2}+\omega_{n}^{2}\right)\end{split} (134)

does not depend on the momentum 𝒒{\bm{q}} since χ0​(q)\chi_{0}(q) does not enter the equation. Since the prefactor drops out within the analytical continuation, this determinant exactly corresponds to the case of free bosons discussed in Appendix E.3, whereby the bosonic energy is given by α⁡(n)\alpha(n). Consequently, the CT contribution to the grand potential is given by

ΩC​T,c(2)|U=0=α2+Tlog(1−e−α/T)→α2.\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,c}\Big|_{U=0}=\frac{\alpha}{2}+T\log\left(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha/T}\right)\rightarrow\frac{\alpha}{2}. (135)

The last equation holds in the limit of low temperatures, which we only consider here. Finite temperature corrections are exponentially small at T≪αT\ll\alpha. We have verified that this result is basis independent: Applying the d,d∗d,d^{*} basis changes the determinant only by a constant factor that drops out in the analytic continuation. Moreover, the determinant of the 6×66\times 6 charge matrix that adds (e,α)(e,\alpha) to the fluctuation basis also differs only by a constant factor. At U=0U=0: detℳc6×6=e¯2​detℳc4×4\det\mathcal{M}_{c}^{6\times 6}=\overline{e}^{2}\det\mathcal{M}_{c}^{4\times 4}, such that the CT fluctuation contribution is also independent of that basis choice.

F.2.2 High frequency contribution

According to Eq. (39), the HFC for the charge sector is given by

ΩH​F​C,c(2)=−U2−32​(α−β0)−2​zH​F​C,c​z0​ε0=−32​α+4n⁡(2−n)​ε0|U=0=−α2,\displaystyle\begin{split}\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,c}&=-\frac{U}{2}-\frac{3}{2}\left(\alpha-\beta_{0}\right)-2z_{HFC,c}z_{0}\varepsilon_{0}\\ &=-\frac{3}{2}\alpha+\frac{4}{n(2-n)}\varepsilon_{0}\Bigg|_{U=0}=-\frac{\alpha}{2},\end{split} (136)

which can be verified by inserting the non-interacting MF solution into the expression for zH​F​C,cz_{HFC,c} given by Eq. (40). In contrast to the spin sector, the CT and HFC contributions do not vanish independently, but their sum

Ωc(2)|U=0=ΩC​T,c(2)|U=0+ΩH​F​C,c(2)|U=0=0\Omega^{(2)}_{c}\Big|_{U=0}=\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,c}\Big|_{U=0}+\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,c}\Big|_{U=0}=0 (137)

is zero, such that there are no charge fluctuation contributions at U=0U=0. We note that the above cancellation does not hold any more at temperatures of the order of α\alpha. At such high temperatures the Gaussian approximation breaks down and the interaction of fluctuations becomes important.

Appendix G Fluctuation corrections with nearest-neighbor interaction VV

We calculate the CT and HFC fluctuation contributions wrt. the nearest-neighbor density-density interaction

HV=V​∑<i​j>n^i​n^j,H^{V}=V\sum_{<ij>}\hat{n}_{i}\hat{n}_{j}, (138)

where n^i=∑σfi,σ†​fi,σ=2​di2+p0,i2+𝒑i2\hat{n}_{i}=\sum_{\sigma}f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f^{\vphantom{\dagger}}_{i,\sigma}=2d_{i}^{2}+p_{0,i}^{2}+{\bm{p}}^{2}_{i}. As shown in Ref. [51], the MF solution for the bosons is invariant under this interaction. Only the chemical potential and the constraint parameter β0\beta_{0} change according to

β0\displaystyle\beta_{0} =β0|V=0+4​V​n,\displaystyle=\beta_{0}\Big|_{V=0}+4Vn, (139)
μ0\displaystyle\mu_{0} =μ0|V=0+4​V​n.\displaystyle=\mu_{0}\Big|_{V=0}+4Vn. (140)

For the bosonic representation of the charge density n^i=2​di2+p0,i2+𝒑i2\hat{n}_{i}=2d_{i}^{2}+p_{0,i}^{2}+{\bm{p}}^{2}_{i} that must be considered in the HFC, the MF solution of the Lagrange multiplier α\alpha remains invariant.

G.1 High frequency contribution

As we show in the following, the HFC is independent of VV. We expand Eq. (138) in anlogy to the previous HFC derivation

HV→4​V​n​(2​d†​d+p0†​p0+𝒑†​𝒑).H^{V}\rightarrow 4Vn(2d^{\dagger}d+p_{0}^{\dagger}p^{\vphantom{\dagger}}_{0}+{\bm{p}}^{\dagger}{\bm{p}}). (141)

The HFC from this term is inferred by replacing the number operators by, e.g., d†​d→−12d^{\dagger}d\rightarrow-\frac{1}{2}.

G.1.1 Spin sector

The HFC from Eq. (141) for the spin sector with the fields p1,p2,p3p_{1},p_{2},p_{3} is given by −32​4​V​n-\frac{3}{2}4Vn. With the additional shift of β0\beta_{0} given by Eq. (139) and the solution at V=0V=0 given by Eq. (85), we find

ΩH​F​C,s(2)​(V)=ΩH​F​C,s(2)​(V=0),\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,s}(V)=\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,s}(V=0), (142)

i.e., independent of VV. Notice that zH​F​C,3​sz_{HFC,3s} is independent of VV since the MF value of e,d,p0,𝒑e,d,p_{0},{\bm{p}} does not depend on VV.

G.1.2 Charge sector

The HFC from Eq. (141) for the charge sector with the fields d,e,p0d,e,p_{0} is given by −32​4​V​n-\frac{3}{2}4Vn. With the additional shift of β0\beta_{0} given by Eq. (139) and the solution at V=0V=0 given by Eq. (94), we again find

ΩH​F​C,c(2)​(V)=ΩH​F​C,c(2)​(V=0).\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,c}(V)=\Omega^{(2)}_{HFC,c}(V=0). (143)

Notice that zH​F​C,cz_{HFC,c} is independent of VV since the MF value of e,d,p0,𝒑e,d,p_{0},{\bm{p}} does not depend on VV.

G.2 Continuous time contribution

As we show below, the CT contribution of the charge sector depends on VV.

G.2.1 Spin sector

In Ref. [51] it has been shown that the (transversal) spin channel of the CT fluctuation matrix does not depend on VV. Consequently ΩC​T,s\Omega_{CT,s} is independent of VV.

G.2.2 Charge sector

As shown in Ref. [51], the CT fluctuation matrix employs additional frequency-independent matrix elements in the charge sector that are proportional to VV. In the basis (d1,d2,p0,β0)(d_{1},d_{2},p_{0},\beta_{0}) applied previously, these are given by

ℳcV​(𝒒)=V​(8​d2​f​(𝒒)04​d​p0​f​(𝒒)000004​d​p0​f​(𝒒)02​p02​f​(𝒒)00000),\mathcal{M}_{c}^{V}({\bm{q}})=V\begin{pmatrix}8d^{2}f({\bm{q}})&0&4dp_{0}f({\bm{q}})&0\\ 0&0&0&0\\ 4dp_{0}f({\bm{q}})&0&2p_{0}^{2}f({\bm{q}})&0\\ 0&0&0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}, (144)

where

f⁡(𝒒)=2​(cos⁡qx+cos⁡qy)f({\bm{q}})=2(\cos q_{x}+\cos q_{y}) (145)

is the form-factor for the nearest-neighbor interaction that can be generalized to longer-ranged interactions [51]. Eq. (144) already accounts for the shift of β0\beta_{0} such that the total charge fluctuation matrix for U,VU,V is given by

ℳcU,V=ℳc​(q)|V=0+ℳcV​(𝒒),\mathcal{M}_{c}^{U,V}=\mathcal{M}_{c}(q)\Big|_{V=0}+\mathcal{M}^{V}_{c}({\bm{q}}), (146)

where ℳc​(q)\mathcal{M}_{c}(q) is given by Eq. (73). At U=0U=0, the total charge determinant is given by

detℳcU,V|U=0=−p02​[1+V​f​(𝒒)​χ0​(q)]​[ωn2+α2].\det\mathcal{M}_{c}^{U,V}\big|_{U=0}=-p_{0}^{2}\left[1+Vf({\bm{q}})\chi_{0}(q)\right]\left[\omega_{n}^{2}+\alpha^{2}\right]. (147)

The free particle contribution α2+ωn2\alpha^{2}+\omega_{n}^{2} can be separated and cancels with the HFC such that

Ω(2)​(V)|U=0=1N​∑𝒒12​T​∑i​ωnln⁡[1+V​f​(𝒒)​χ0​(𝒒,i​ωn)].\Omega^{(2)}(V)\big|_{U=0}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bm{q}}\frac{1}{2}T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\ln\left[1+Vf({\bm{q}})\chi_{0}({\bm{q}},i\omega_{n})\right]. (148)

The charge susceptibility at U=0U=0 adopts an RPA-like form

χc​(q)|U=0=χ01+V​f​(𝒒)​χ0​(q).\chi_{c}(q)\Big|_{U=0}=\frac{\chi_{0}}{1+Vf({\bm{q}})\chi_{0}(q)}. (149)

G.3 Results

Fig. 12shows the free energy as a function of VV for U=2U=2 near half-filling. The charge-channel fluctuation contribution increases with VV, whereas the spin contribution is agnostic to VV.

Appendix H Numerical evaluation of the CT contribution

There are three available methods to numerically evaluate the fluctuation corrections that have been derived in the main text, summarized by the following equations:

(i) numerical evaluation of the Matsubara sum according to

ΩC​T,s/c(2)=as/c2TN∑𝒒∑i​ωnlndetℳs/c(q).\displaystyle\begin{split}\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,s/c}&=\frac{a_{s/c}}{2}\frac{T}{N}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\sum_{\mathrm{i}\omega_{n}}\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}(q).\end{split} (150)

(ii) numerical integration of the phase of the fluctuation determinant along the real axis according to

ΩC​T,s/c(2)=as/c2​1N​∑𝒒∫0∞d​ωπ​coth⁡(ω2​T)​arg⁡(detℳs/c),\displaystyle\begin{split}\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,s/c}&=\frac{a_{s/c}}{2}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{\pi}\coth\left(\frac{\omega}{2T}\right)\arg\left(\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}\right),\end{split} (151)

using that the functions lndetℳs/c\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c} are analytic on the complex plane except for the real axis and satisfy

lndetℳs/c(𝒒,ω+i0+)\displaystyle\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}({\bm{q}},\omega+\mathrm{i}0^{+}) =[lndetℳs/c(𝒒,ω−i0+)]∗,\displaystyle=\left[\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}({\bm{q}},\omega-\mathrm{i}0^{+})\right]^{*}, (152)
lndetℳs/c(𝒒,ω+i0+)\displaystyle\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}({\bm{q}},\omega+\mathrm{i}0^{+}) =lndetℳs/c(𝒒,−ω−i0+),\displaystyle=\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}({\bm{q}},-\omega-\mathrm{i}0^{+}), (153)

where the second identity holds because the determinants are even functions in ωn\omega_{n}. Then the integration contour is moved to infinity and thereby wrapped around the real axis.

(iii) numerical integration along the real axis after partial integration according to

ΩC​T,s/c(2)=as/c2​1N​∑𝒒∫0∞2​d​ωπ​f​(ω)​Ss/c​(ω),\displaystyle\begin{split}\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,s/c}&=\frac{a_{s/c}}{2}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{2d\omega}{\pi}f(\omega)S_{s/c}(\omega),\end{split} (154)

where

Ss/c​(𝒒,ω)=−Ds/c′∂ωDs/c′′+Ds/c′′∂ωD′|detℳs/c|2,f⁡(ω)=ω2+Tlog|1−e−ω/T|,\displaystyle\begin{split}S_{s/c}({\bm{q}},\omega)&=\frac{-D_{s/c}^{\prime}\partial_{\omega}D_{s/c}^{\prime\prime}+D_{s/c}^{\prime\prime}\partial_{\omega}D^{\prime}}{|\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}|^{2}},\\ f(\omega)&=\frac{\omega}{2}+T\log\big|1-\mathrm{e}^{-\omega/T}\big|,\end{split} (155)

and

Ds/c′=Re​detℳs/c​(𝒒,ω+i0),Ds/c′′=Im​detℳs/c​(𝒒,ω+i0).\displaystyle\begin{split}D_{s/c}^{\prime}&=\text{Re}\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}({\bm{q}},\omega+\mathrm{i}0),\\ D_{s/c}^{\prime\prime}&=\text{Im}\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}({\bm{q}},\omega+\mathrm{i}0).\end{split} (156)

For each approach, there are numerical subtleties that we elaborate in the following. We are able to recover the same result with either of the methods, but there are substantial differences in the rate of convergence. The Matsubara summation is clearly favored over the frequency integrals. This is because the numerical error generated by a finite value of the convergence parameter η>0\eta>0, which is required for the integral method, is significant due to the overall small energy scale of the fluctuation corrections (in the order of 10−210^{-2}). Therefore, we demand the numerical error to be Δ​Ω(2)≪10−3\Delta\Omega^{(2)}\ll 10^{-3}. To achieve this precision, we require η≲0.001\eta\lesssim 0.001, which necessitates a very large number of fermionic momenta N𝒌≳1024N_{\bm{k}}\gtrsim 1024 because the imaginary part of the bare susceptibility Im⁡χ0\Im\chi_{0} converges rather slowly for such small η\eta. This problem does not occur for the Matsubara summation, since there is no convergence parameter required, and the bare susceptibility is a real-valued quantity in that case. Also, the Matsubara sum can efficiently be extrapolated to infinity, as we show below.

The sum over the bosonic momenta 𝒒{\bm{q}} with a total number of N𝒒N_{\bm{q}} also needs to be carried out numerically over the Brillouin zone (BZ). It can be reduced to 1/81/8 of the BZ by exploiting the c​4​vc4v symmetry (4-fold rotation and mirror symmetry). There are no particular subtleties as in the case of the Matsubara summation, but N𝒒N_{\bm{q}} needs to be large enough to encompass incommensurate fluctuation contributions, i.e, N𝒒≳8×8N_{\bm{q}}\gtrsim 8\times 8 (compare subsection V.3).

H.1 Numerical evaluation of the Matsubara sum

In Eq. (150), we need to perform the summation ∑i​ωn=∑n=−∞∞\sum_{\mathrm{i}\omega_{n}}=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} over the bosonic Matsubara frequencies ωn=2​π​n​T\omega_{n}=2\pi nT, where TT is the temperature. Since the fluctuation determinant is symmetric in ωn\omega_{n}, this sum can be reduced to n≥0n\geq 0, whereby every point except n=0n=0 is counted twice. The sum needs to be evaluated at finite temperature but can easily be extrapolated to T→0T\rightarrow 0. We apply T=0.01T=0.01, since the leading-order temperature-dependence is quadratic, i.e., the deviation from T=0T=0 is only of the order 10−410^{-4}.

H.1.1 Spin sector

After omitting the pre-factor −p02-p_{0}^{2} that drops out in the analytical continuation method (the sign is irrelevant and depends on the integration direction of the fields around the saddle point), the spin determinant is given by

lndetℳs(q)=ln[χ0(q)/χs(q)]∼as,𝒒/ωn2,\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s}(q)=\ln\left[\chi_{0}(q)/\chi_{s}(q)\right]\sim a_{s,{\bm{q}}}/\omega_{n}^{2}, (157)

the asymptotic behavior of which guarantees convergence of the Matsubara sum. It may be evaluated approximately using a suitable cutoff ωnc=2​π​T​nc\omega_{n_{c}}=2\pi Tn_{c}. The proportionality factor is determined by as,𝒒=limωn→∞lndetℳs(𝒒,ωnc)ωnc2a_{s,{\bm{q}}}=\lim_{\omega_{n}\rightarrow\infty}\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s}({\bm{q}},\omega_{n_{c}})\omega_{n_{c}}^{2}. The asymptotic behavior can be summed up exactly as

T∑i​ωnlndetℳs(𝒒,ωn)=Tlndetℳs(𝒒,0)+2T∑n=1nclndetℳs(𝒒,ωn)+Tas,𝒒4​π2​T2ψ(1)(nc+1)+O(1/nc3),T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s}({\bm{q}},\omega_{n})=T\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s}({\bm{q}},0)+2T\sum_{n=1}^{n_{c}}\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{s}({\bm{q}},\omega_{n})+T\frac{a_{s,{\bm{q}}}}{4\pi^{2}T^{2}}\psi^{(1)}(n_{c}+1)+O(1/n_{c}^{3}), (158)

where

ψ(1)​(n)=∑x=n∞1x2\psi^{(1)}(n)=\sum_{x=n}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}} (159)

is the Polygamma function and nc→∞n_{c}\rightarrow\infty. In the numerical evaluation, we apply nc=3000n_{c}=3000, ωc=2​π​T​nc\omega_{c}=2\pi Tn_{c}, whereby the error due to the cutoff is ≲10−5\lesssim 10^{-5}.

H.1.2 Charge sector

The charge sector is formally divergent in the ill-defined continuum limit, since

lndetℳc(q)∼ac,𝒒(ω𝒒2+ωn2)\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{c}(q)\sim a_{c,{\bm{q}}}\left(\omega_{{\bm{q}}}^{2}+\omega_{n}^{2}\right) (160)

for ωn→∞\omega_{n}\rightarrow\infty. We may identify this behavior as a harmonic oscillator-like contribution of bosons of frequency ω𝒒\omega_{{\bm{q}}}. The free energy of such a system is known to be

Ωfree(𝒒)=ω𝒒/2+Tln(1−e−ω𝒒/T).\Omega_{\text{free}}({\bm{q}})=\omega_{{\bm{q}}}/2+T\ln\left(1-e^{-\omega_{{\bm{q}}}/T}\right). (161)

We will separate the divergent part by fitting the above behavior beyond a cutoff ncn_{c}

T∑i​ωnlndetℳc(𝒒,ωn)\displaystyle T\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\ln\det\mathcal{M}_{c}({\bm{q}},\omega_{n}) =T​ln⁡detℳc​(𝒒,0)ac,𝒒​ω𝒒2+2​T​∑n=1∞ln⁡detℳc​(𝒒,ωn)ac,𝒒​(ω𝒒2+ωn2)+ac,𝒒​Ωfree​(𝒒).\displaystyle=T\ln\frac{\det\mathcal{M}_{c}({\bm{q}},0)}{a_{c,{\bm{q}}}\omega_{\bm{q}}^{2}}+2T\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\ln\frac{\det\mathcal{M}_{c}({\bm{q}},\omega_{n})}{a_{c,{\bm{q}}}\left(\omega_{\bm{q}}^{2}+\omega_{n}^{2}\right)}+a_{c,{\bm{q}}}\Omega_{\text{free}}({\bm{q}}). (162)

In the numerical evaluation, we use a cutoff n=nc≈3000n=n_{c}\approx 3000 for the summation on Matsubara frequencies. The parameters a𝒒,ω𝒒a_{\bm{q}},\omega_{\bm{q}} are determined by the charge fluctuation determinant around the cutoff, where we define ω1=ωnc−1,D1,𝒒=detℳc​(𝒒,ω1)\omega_{1}=\omega_{n_{c}-1},D_{1,{\bm{q}}}=\det\mathcal{M}_{c}({\bm{q}},\omega_{1}) and ω2=ωnc,D2,𝒒=detℳc​(𝒒,ω2)\omega_{2}=\omega_{n_{c}},D_{2,{\bm{q}}}=\det\mathcal{M}_{c}({\bm{q}},\omega_{2}), yielding

a𝒒\displaystyle a_{\bm{q}} =D1,𝒒−D2,𝒒ω12−ω22,\displaystyle=\frac{D_{1,{\bm{q}}}-D_{2,{\bm{q}}}}{\omega_{1}^{2}-\omega_{2}^{2}}, (163)
ω𝒒\displaystyle\omega_{\bm{q}} =D2,𝒒​ω12−D1,𝒒​ω22D1,𝒒−D2,𝒒,\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{D_{2,{\bm{q}}}\omega_{1}^{2}-D_{1,{\bm{q}}}\omega_{2}^{2}}{D_{1,{\bm{q}}}-D_{2,{\bm{q}}}}}, (164)

such that ln⁡[detℳc​(𝒒,ωnc)/a𝒒​(ω𝒒2+ωnc2)]=0\ln\left[\det\mathcal{M}_{c}({\bm{q}},\omega_{n_{c}})/a_{\bm{q}}\left(\omega_{\bm{q}}^{2}+\omega_{n_{c}}^{2}\right)\right]=0 at the cutoff.

H.2 Numerical evaluation of the frequency integral

The integration along the real axis needs to be performed with care. First, the susceptibility χ0​(𝒒,ω+i​0)\chi_{0}({\bm{q}},\omega+i0) entering the fluctuation matrix must be evaluated numerically, involving integration on 𝒌{\bm{k}} over the Brillouin zone. This may be done by keeping a finite imaginary part η\eta of the frequency, ω→ω+i​η\omega\rightarrow\omega+i\eta to ensure convergence of the numerical integration. The parameters η\eta, the step size d​ωd\omega of the discretized frequency and the temperature TT need to be chosen judiciously. We choose both, d​ω≪η≪Td\omega\ll\eta\ll T and sufficiently high number of points N𝒒,N𝒌N_{\bm{q}},N_{\bm{k}} in momentum space.

H.2.1 Phase integration

The CT fluctuation contribution to the partition function is determined by integrating the phase of the fluctuation determinant weighted by the Bose function

ΩC​T,s/c(2)=as/c​1N​∑𝒒∫0∞d​ω2​π​coth⁡(ω2​T)​arg⁡(detℳs/c).\displaystyle\begin{split}\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,s/c}&=a_{s/c}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\coth\left(\frac{\omega}{2T}\right)\arg\left(\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}\right).\\ \end{split} (165)

where arg⁡(detℳs/c)\arg\left(\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}\right) is the phase of detℳs/c\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}. The phase of the spin determinant is given by the usual expression

arg⁡(detℳs)=arctan⁡(Ds′′/Ds′)\displaystyle\arg\left(\det\mathcal{M}_{s}\right)=\arctan\left(D_{s}^{\prime\prime}/D_{s}^{\prime}\right) (166)

where we defined the real and imaginary parts of the determinant detℳs/c=Ds,c′+i​Ds,c′′\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}=D_{s,c}^{\prime}+iD_{s,c}^{\prime\prime}. The charge determinant features roots on the real axis such that the continuity of the phase needs to be recovered by the correct addition of π\pi. For T=0T=0, this is achieved by

arg⁡(detℳs)\displaystyle\arg\left(\det\mathcal{M}_{s}\right) =arctan⁡(Ds′′/Ds′),\displaystyle=\,\,\,\arctan\left(D_{s}^{\prime\prime}/D_{s}^{\prime}\right), (167)
arg⁡(detℳc)\displaystyle\arg\left(\det\mathcal{M}_{c}\right) ={arctan⁡(Dc′′/Dc′)if ​Dc′>0,Dc′′>0arctan⁡(Dc′′/Dc′)+πelse.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\arctan\left(D_{c}^{\prime\prime}/D_{c}^{\prime}\right)\qquad\,\,\,\text{if }D_{c}^{\prime}>0,D_{c}^{\prime\prime}>0\\ \arctan\left(D_{c}^{\prime\prime}/D_{c}^{\prime}\right)+\pi\quad\text{else}.\end{cases}

H.2.2 Partial integration

Alternatively, we can perform a partial integration, which avoids the issue with the continuity of the phase:

ΩC​T,s/c(2)\displaystyle\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,s/c} =as/c​1N​∑𝒒∫0∞d​ωπ​f​(ω)​Ss/c​(ω),\displaystyle=a_{s/c}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\bm{q}}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{d\omega}{\pi}f(\omega)S_{s/c}(\omega), (168)

where we define the functions

Ss/c​(𝒒,ω)=−Im​∂ωdetℳs/c​(𝒒,ω+i​0+)detℳs/c=−Ds/c′∂ωDs/c′′+Ds/c′′∂ωD′|detℳs/c|2​f​(ω),f⁡(ω)=ω2+Tlog|1−e−ω/T|.\displaystyle\begin{split}S_{s/c}({\bm{q}},\omega)&=-\text{Im}\frac{\partial_{\omega}\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}({\bm{q}},\omega+i0^{+})}{\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}}\\ &=\frac{-D_{s/c}^{\prime}\partial_{\omega}D_{s/c}^{\prime\prime}+D_{s/c}^{\prime\prime}\partial_{\omega}D^{\prime}}{|\det\mathcal{M}_{s/c}|^{2}}f(\omega),\\ f(\omega)&=\frac{\omega}{2}+T\log\big|1-\mathrm{e}^{-\omega/T}\big|.\end{split} (169)

However, the integration converges slower than the phase integration due to the numerical derivative that needs to be evaluated. Due to η→0\eta\rightarrow 0 remaining finite within the numerics, Eq. (168) features a logarithmic divergence for ω→∞\omega\rightarrow\infty in the charge sector. Convergence can be recovered by introducing a cutoff ωc\omega_{c} of the integral that is chosen such that the first order of its η\eta-dependence vanishes, i.e., ΩC​T,c(2)=a+b​η3+𝒪⁡(η5)\Omega^{(2)}_{CT,c}=a+b\eta^{3}+\mathcal{O}(\eta^{5}).

H.3 Comparison of HFC and CT contribution

In Fig. 13 and Fig. 14, we show the results for the HFC and CT contribution separately in the lower panels, as well as their sum, that is, the total result, in the upper panels. In case of spin, the total fluctuation contribution is reduced to less than 3%3\% of the CT result with the addition of the HFC. For the charge sector, the situation is even more extreme, since the CT part is of the order of α¯\overline{\alpha} (e.g. for n=1,U=0,t′=0n=1,U=0,t^{\prime}=0, α¯=64/π2\overline{\alpha}=64/\pi^{2}) and the correct non-interacting limit is only recovered with the addition of the HFC, compare Appendix F. Here, with the addition of HFC, the total charge fluctuation result is reduced to less than 0.25%0.25\% of the CT value. These results illustrate the huge errors caused by the CT approximation that, by all means, need to be corrected with the addition of HFCs to recover an error-free functional integral representation.

Appendix I Tables of numerical results

Here, we provide the numerical values of the SRIKR+ (mean field plus fluctuation) results that are shown within Fig. 3 and Fig. 4. The fluctuation calculation is done for the grand canonical ensemble ,i.e., we use the chemical potential μ0\mu_{0} as an input parameter and calculate the density nt​o​t=n(0)+ns(2)+nc(2)n_{tot}=n^{(0)}+n^{(2)}_{s}+n^{(2)}_{c} afterwards. The data shown in Table 1 and Table 2 is extrapolated to fractions of the total filling with negligible error. The total free energy is given by the sum of the mean field and fluctuation contribution Ftot=F(0)+Fs(2)+Fc(2)F_{\text{tot}}=F^{(0)}+F^{(2)}_{s}+F^{(2)}_{c}.

Our method requires a finite temperature because of the Matsubara summation. We applied T=0.01T=0.01 as zero temperature limit. This causes a difference of less than 10−410^{-4} wrt. to the free energy, since we find the temperature coefficient γ≲1\gamma\lesssim 1. The numerical difference of the free energy at n=1n=1 calculated for t=±0.2t=\pm 0.2 is of the order of only 10−610^{-6} (the result must be identical due to particle-hole symmetry). This underlines the effectiveness of our numerical calculations.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
